03 Mood and cognition · class card

Cognitive agents

cholinesterase inhibitors · donepezil · rivastigmine · galantamine · memantine

Key point
  • Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine block acetylcholinesterase more acetylcholine modest gain in cognition, no change in the course
  • Memantine blocks N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors less glutamate excitotoxicity; for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, often added to a cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Extra acetylcholine brings nausea, diarrhea and weight loss and slows the heart bradycardia, heart block, syncope; anticholinergic drugs work against these drugs
Drugs

Donepezil Aricept: once a day, in the evening; every stage of Alzheimer disease

Rivastigmine Exelon: by mouth or a daily skin patch; Alzheimer disease and mild-to-moderate Parkinson disease dementia LabelOne patch at a time, replaced every 24 hours; most medication errors reported on the label were an old patch left on or several worn at once, and some needed a hospital stay.

Galantamine: also modulates nicotinic receptors, which adds to acetylcholine release

Memantine: uncompetitive, open-channel NMDA receptor antagonist; moderate to severe disease

Mechanism

Alzheimer disease: the nucleus basalis of Meynert loses choline acetyltransferase low acetylcholine

Acetylcholinesterase blocked, reversibly less acetylcholine broken down more at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors

The same surplus outside the brain gut and bladder smooth muscle contract, vagal tone slows the heart

Glutamate keeps NMDA receptors open calcium entry excitotoxicity; memantine plugs the open channel

Uses

Alzheimer disease: a cholinesterase inhibitor, the three about equally effective; memantine for moderate to severe disease, alone or added

Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia): cholinesterase inhibitors first, for cognition, attention and visual hallucinations

Parkinson disease dementia: cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine

No data to support use in mild cognitive impairment, and no help in delirium caused by a drug

Adverse effects

Cholinesterase inhibitors: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia and weight loss; insomnia, dizziness, muscle cramps, urinary incontinence LabelOften transient; a slow dose climb reduces them. On the patch they can force a pause, and long vomiting or diarrhea can dehydrate.

Vagal slowing at the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes may bring bradycardia, heart block or syncope, with or without known conduction disease

More gastric acid ulcer and GI bleeding risk; caution in asthma or obstructive lung disease LabelCholinomimetics may also cause bladder outflow obstruction and may carry some potential for generalized seizures.

Memantine: dizziness, headache, confusion, constipation; hallucinations

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
Anticholinergic drugs, such as oxybutynin or tolterodineEach works against the other; anticholinergic toxicity brings delirium, sedation and hallucinations Avoid unless clinically necessary
Beta-blockers, especially atenolol (rivastigmine label)Additive slowing of the heart, which can bring faintingNot recommended once signs appear
Succinylcholine during anesthesiaMuscle relaxation is alteredExpect it exaggerated: a deeper block
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugsMay add gastric acidWatch for active or hidden bleeding
Metoclopramide (rivastigmine label)Additive extrapyramidal reactionsNot recommended
Memantine with sodium bicarbonate or a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor Memantine labelMemantine with other NMDA antagonists (amantadine, ketamine, dextromethorphan) is unstudied; the label advises caution.Alkaline urine cuts memantine clearance by about 80%: it may accumulateWatch for more adverse effects
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
During treatment, most of all with sick sinus syndrome or other conduction diseasePulse; ask about faintingVagal slowing of the heart
If that check is abnormalElectrocardiogram ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yetBradycardia or heart block
During treatmentAppetite and weightIts gastrointestinal adverse effects
After several monthsDaily function, with the caregiver reportDecides whether to continue or stop
Memantine with severe kidney diseaseCreatinine clearanceSevere impairment: target 5 mg twice daily

Practice
  1. 76-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease began donepezil 2 weeks ago since then nausea, loose stools, and urinary urgency with leaking pulse 58/min · abdomen soft, active bowel sounds · urinalysis normal → More acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors → donepezil blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up and drives gut motility, bladder contraction and vagal slowing of the heart; these effects are often transient and fewer when the dose climbs slowly
  2. 81-year-old man with moderate to severe Alzheimer disease on donepezil a second drug for the dementia was added 3 weeks ago since then dizziness, headache, more confusion and constipation pulse 74/min · moist mouth · pupils normal · bladder not distended → NMDA receptor antagonist → memantine is the drug added to a cholinesterase inhibitor in moderate to severe disease, and dizziness, headache, confusion and constipation are its common effects; his moist mouth, normal pupils and normal pulse argue against a muscarinic antagonist
  3. 79-year-old man with Alzheimer disease, stable on donepezil for a year oxybutynin started 10 days ago for urge incontinence now more forgetful and confused, says his daughter afebrile · dry mouth · pupils 6 mm · urinalysis normal → Anticholinergic effect opposing donepezil → oxybutynin blocks the muscarinic receptors that the extra acetylcholine from donepezil is meant to reach, and anticholinergic drugs bring confusion, dry mouth and wide pupils of their own; urinary incontinence is itself a donepezil effect
